Adding two rear teeth gives **stronger pull, quicker revs and more shifting**, but less speed in each gear—it doesn’t add horsepower.

Assuming your 2023 450 SX-F still has KTM’s stock **13/51 gearing**, going to **13/53** works out to:
- **3.9% more rear-wheel torque** at the same engine torque, and 3.9% higher rpm at the same road speed.
- **3.8% less speed at the same rpm** in each gear.

It helps if you’re between gears or need more drive out of tight corners. On slick ground, that stronger pull can make wheelspin easier.

The bigger sprocket also pulls the axle forward with the same chain, slightly shortening the wheelbase. KTM lists rear options from **47–52 teeth**, so check the aftermarket 53-tooth sprocket’s fitment and whether your chain has enough adjustment before buying.

If you’re only changing gearing, you can reuse a fresh chain provided it has no stiff links, damaged rollers or excessive wear:
- Hold it taut and measure across **17 pins (16 pitches)**: replace at **257 mm (10.1 in)**.
- Replace if the inner plates wear down to **14.0 mm (0.55 in)**.
- Honda’s race replacement schedule is **every 3 races/about 7.5 hours**—passing a wear check isn’t a reason to stretch that schedule.

**Gearing changes wheelbase because a different-size sprocket takes up more or less of the same chain.**

With chain length unchanged:
- **More rear teeth or a bigger front:** axle moves forward, shortening wheelbase.
- **Fewer rear teeth or a smaller front:** axle moves backward, lengthening wheelbase.

On your KTM’s 520 chain, each tooth added moves the axle forward **about 4 mm**; removing a tooth moves it back about the same amount. That’s an engineering estimate from chain pitch, assuming the same chain—not an exact adjustment measurement. Adding two chain links moves the axle back roughly **16 mm**, retaining the same sprockets.

A shorter wheelbase generally turns more quickly and lifts the front more easily. A longer wheelbase generally tracks straighter through fast chop and resists wheelies, but takes more effort to turn tightly. Your KTM’s published wheelbase is **1,493 ± 10 mm (58.8 ± 0.4 in)**.

The important distinction: **a bigger rear sprocket shortens gearing and wheelbase; a smaller front shortens gearing but lengthens wheelbase.** Similar gearing changes can therefore feel different.

After changing sprockets, reset chain slack and wheel alignment before judging handling.
With the same chain, bigger sprockets move the rear axle forward; smaller sprockets move it back. That changes steering and stability as well as gearing.

Pros change fork-tube height to **trade turning response against stability**—and keep the front balanced with the rear.

- **More tube showing above the top clamp:** lowers the front, steepens the steering and generally helps it bite and turn tighter. Too far, and it can tuck or shake at speed.
- **Less tube showing, closer to flush:** raises the front, generally calming the steering in fast, rough sections, but it can push wide in tight corners.

A tight track may favor more tube showing; fast, rough tracks or deep sand often favor less. It isn’t a fixed rule: grip, ruts, braking loads and rear ride height all affect the choice. Pros also change springs and damping between tracks, so fork height helps restore the balance afterward.

On your **2022 CRF250R**, testers consistently report a sensitive, nervous front end, so raising the tubes isn’t automatically an improvement. Common practice is **1–2 mm at a time**, both legs identical, then compare the same corners and rough straight. Keep rear sag consistent while testing—Honda’s standard with the stock shock spring is **105 mm (4.1 in)**.

**Axle forward = quicker handling; axle back = more stability.** On your CRF250R:

- **Forward:** shorter wheelbase, easier direction changes and easier front-wheel lift. The rear suspension can feel slightly firmer because the wheel has less leverage on the shock.
- **Back:** longer wheelbase, calmer through fast chop and whoops, but slower to change direction. More leverage on the shock can give a slightly softer, more settled rear feel.

These are general setup effects—not a guaranteed traction fix. Tire grip, sag and damping still matter more.

Honda lists a **58.1-inch wheelbase** as the stock reference. Don’t move the axle by deliberately tightening or loosening the chain: maintain **65–70 mm (2½–2¾ inches)**, measured with the rear wheel off the ground, chain lifted, from the swingarm’s top surface to the chain-pin center. Meaningful axle-position changes may require a different chain length; keep wheel alignment correct and recheck sag afterward.
Axle forward makes the bike more agile; axle back makes it calmer at speed and gives the rear wheel more leverage on the shock.

**Gentle water and a cold engine are the keys—not blasting every speck off with pressure.**

1. Let the engine and exhaust cool, put the bike securely on its stand and wash out of direct sunlight.
2. Plug the exhaust and protect the airbox opening. If removing the filter, fit a proper wash cover—never leave the intake exposed.
3. Rinse loose dirt off gently. Apply motorcycle cleaner to the **wet bike**, then loosen dirt with a soft brush or sponge. Don’t let cleaner dry on it.
4. Prefer a hose. With a pressure washer, keep the nozzle at least **60 cm (23.6 inches)** away. Never aim it into bearings, seals, electrical connectors, handlebar switches, the intake or control-cable entries. Don’t blast the chain.
5. Rinse gently and dry thoroughly. Remove the exhaust plug and any intake covering; make sure the clean, oiled filter is correctly fitted before starting.
6. At walking pace in a clear area, apply the brakes gently several times. **If normal braking doesn’t return, stop and inspect before riding.** Once they work normally, take a short easy ride to warm the engine and evaporate hidden moisture.
7. Let it cool, lubricate pivots and the chain, and protect bare metal. Keep sprays off brake discs, pads, tires and the exhaust. Look for leaks, cracks and loose parts while it’s clean.

Test only one change over the same exit for a few laps; undo it if drive gets worse. Several testers found this generation’s shock soft, so automatically softening it can make matters worse.
